title: Three Primes and a Ratio
statement: For a positive integer $m$, let $\sigma(m)$ denote the sum of the positive divisors of $m$, and let $\varphi(m)$ denote the number of positive integers at most $m$ that are coprime to $m$. Let $N$ be the largest positive integer that is a product of three distinct primes and for which $\frac{\sigma(N)}{\varphi(N)}$ is an integer. Find the remainder when $N$ is divided by $1000$.
hints: Write $N = pqr$ with primes $p < q < r$, and express $\frac{\sigma(N)}{\varphi(N)}$ as a product of three factors, one for each prime. Look at how the factor for a prime changes as the prime grows.

Use bounding. The factor $f(x) = \frac{x+1}{x-1}$ is greater than $1$ and decreases as $x$ grows, so fixing the smaller primes traps the product $f(p)f(q)f(r)$ in a short interval. If that interval contains no integer, the choice of smaller primes is impossible.

With $f(x) = \frac{x+1}{x-1}$, fix $p < q$ and let $c = f(p)f(q)$. The product satisfies $c < c \cdot f(r) \le c \cdot f(q')$, where $q'$ is the next prime after $q$. An integer lies in this range only for the pairs $(p, q)$ equal to $(2,3)$, $(2,5)$, $(2,11)$, $(3,5)$, $(3,7)$ and $(5,11)$. For each pair and each integer $k$ in the range, solve $f(r) = \frac{k}{c}$, keep the prime values of $r$, and compare the resulting products $pqr$.
solution: Write $N = pqr$ with primes $p < q < r$. Then $\sigma(N) = (p+1)(q+1)(r+1)$ and $\varphi(N) = (p-1)(q-1)(r-1)$, so $$\dfrac{\sigma(N)}{\varphi(N)} = f(p)f(q)f(r), \qquad \text{where } f(x) = \dfrac{x+1}{x-1} = 1 + \dfrac{2}{x-1}.$$ The function $f$ is strictly decreasing for $x > 1$ and always exceeds $1$. Its values at the first primes are $f(2) = 3$, $f(3) = 2$, $f(5) = \frac{3}{2}$, $f(7) = \frac{4}{3}$, $f(11) = \frac{6}{5}$, $f(13) = \frac{7}{6}$ and $f(17) = \frac{9}{8}$. Also $f(r) = g$ has the unique solution $r = \frac{g+1}{g-1}$. Let $c = f(p)f(q)$ and $k = c \cdot f(r)$, which must be an integer. Then $k > c$, and $k \le c \cdot f(q')$, where $q'$ is the next prime after $q$. Once $k$ is known, $f(r) = \frac{k}{c}$ determines $r$. Suppose $p \ge 7$. Then $1 < k \le \frac{4}{3} \cdot \frac{6}{5} \cdot \frac{7}{6} = \frac{28}{15} < 2$, which is impossible. So $p \in \{2, 3, 5\}$. Suppose $p = 5$. If $q \ge 13$, then $1 < k \le \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{7}{6} \cdot \frac{9}{8} = \frac{63}{32} < 2$, which is impossible. If $q = 7$, then $c = 2$ and $2 < k \le \frac{12}{5}$, which contains no integer. If $q = 11$, then $c = \frac{9}{5}$ and $\frac{9}{5} < k \le \frac{21}{10}$, so $k = 2$. This gives $f(r) = \frac{10}{9}$, so $r = 19$, which is prime, and $N = 5 \cdot 11 \cdot 19 = 1045$. Suppose $p = 3$. If $q \ge 11$, then $2 < k \le 2 \cdot \frac{6}{5} \cdot \frac{7}{6} = \frac{14}{5} < 3$, which is impossible. If $q = 5$, then $c = 3$ and $3 < k \le 4$, so $k = 4$, $f(r) = \frac{4}{3}$, $r = 7$ and $N = 105$. If $q = 7$, then $c = \frac{8}{3}$ and $\frac{8}{3} < k \le \frac{16}{5}$, so $k = 3$, $f(r) = \frac{9}{8}$, $r = 17$ and $N = 357$. Suppose $p = 2$. If $q \ge 13$, then $3 < k \le 3 \cdot \frac{7}{6} \cdot \frac{9}{8} = \frac{63}{16} < 4$, which is impossible. If $q = 3$, then $c = 6$ and $6 < k \le 9$. The values $k = 7, 8, 9$ give $r = 13, 7, 5$, so $N = 78, 42, 30$. If $q = 5$, then $c = \frac{9}{2}$ and $\frac{9}{2} < k \le 6$. The values $k = 5, 6$ give $r = 19, 7$, so $N = 190, 70$. If $q = 7$, then $c = 4$ and $4 < k \le \frac{24}{5}$, which contains no integer. If $q = 11$, then $c = \frac{18}{5}$ and $\frac{18}{5} < k \le \frac{21}{5}$, so $k = 4$, $f(r) = \frac{10}{9}$, $r = 19$ and $N = 418$. The valid values of $N$ are therefore $30, 42, 70, 78, 105, 190, 357, 418$ and $1045$. The largest is $N = 1045$, where $\frac{\sigma(N)}{\varphi(N)} = \frac{1440}{720} = 2$. The remainder when $N$ is divided by $1000$ is $45$. Why this works. bounding, casework, multiplicativity: the multiplicative ratio splits into decreasing factors, so trapping it between consecutive integers leaves only finitely many prime cases to check.
